result.summary: Ovid presents Pythagoras, a Samian exile at Crotona, teaching a crowd. He argues against eating meat, since souls pass between bodies, and he says all things change. His examples are the seasons, the elements, rivers, lands, animals and cities, and he ends by urging mercy toward animals.

scenes.title: Pythagoras the Samian exile
scenes.summary: Pythagoras, a voluntary exile from Samos, studies nature with his mind and teaches the silent crowds at Crotona.

scenes.title: Against eating animal flesh
scenes.summary: Pythagoras urges people to live on the earth's produce, recalls the Golden age, and pities the sheep and oxen killed in sacrifice.
scenes.stakes: Animals face slaughter, and humans risk wickedness by eating their own tillers and kindred.

scenes.title: Souls migrate, all things change
scenes.summary: He says souls do not die but pass into new bodies, as he was once Euphorbus. He compares change to time, the seasons and the ages of life.
scenes.stakes: Humans fear death needlessly and may kill their own kin.

scenes.title: Elements, lands and waters change
scenes.summary: The four elements change into one another. Seas become land, rivers vanish or turn strange, and Aetna will one day burn out.

scenes.title: Marvels of living creatures
scenes.summary: He cites animals that are born from rotting matter or change form, and the Phoenix that renews itself.

scenes.title: Rise and fall of cities
scenes.summary: Troy, Sparta, Thebes and Athens have fallen, while Rome rises as Helenus foretold to Aeneas.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas fears for his safety as Troy sinks.

scenes.title: Closing plea for mercy
scenes.summary: Pythagoras asks people to spare animals that may house kindred souls and to kill only what is harmful.
scenes.stakes: Humans risk cruelty close to murder.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of Venus, whose doves are mentioned.

notable_quotes.reason: Concise statement of the central doctrine: everything changes and nothing perishes.
Time is compared to a flowing river, a famous image of change.

analysis.text: Change is the unifying theme of the Metamorphoses, and Pythagoras makes it a philosophy, covering the seasons, elements, lands and empires.
Ovid draws on Pythagorean ideas of vegetarianism and reincarnation, and flatters Rome by presenting its rise as part of the cosmic flux.

legacy.text: Pythagoras's speech helped to spread vegetarianism, which was long called the Pythagorean diet in Europe.
The phrase 'all things flow' and Ovid's account of the Phoenix influenced later literature.

fun_facts.text: Ovid wrote his Pythagoras speech in the first century AD, centuries after the philosopher lived, so the teachings are a Roman reconstruction.

language_notes.text: The Samian is Pythagoras, born on the island of Samos. He left because of the tyranny of Polycrates, according to tradition.
The syntax is muddled: the crowds 'wondered at' the revealed origins, meaning he taught them about cosmic origins and causes while they listened in awed silence.
'Redolent' means fragrant; the honey carries the scent of thyme blossom.
Armenia was proverbially a land of fierce tigers in Roman literature.
The Cyclops, such as Polyphemus, were savage giants who ate human flesh; eating animals is likened to their cannibal habits.
The goat is sacrificed to Bacchus, god of wine, as punishment for eating his vines.
'Delphic' refers to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi; Pythagoras claims prophetic authority.
Atlas was the Titan who held up the sky on his shoulders.
Styx is the river of the Underworld; "shades" are the ghosts of the dead living there.
Euphorbus was a Trojan wounded by Patroclus and killed by Menelaus, the younger son of Atreus, in the Iliad. Pythagoras claims to be his reincarnation.
Menelaus was said to have dedicated Euphorbus' shield in Juno's temple at Argos, which proves Pythagoras' claim of past life.
Lucifer means "light-bringer", the morning star; Aurora, dawn, is called daughter of Pallas, a Titan, not Minerva.
Diana here stands for the moon, which she personifies.
Milo of Croton was a famous athlete and wrestler, proverbially strong.
The daughter of Tyndarus is Helen, famed for beauty, carried off first by Theseus and later by Paris.
"As many" means two more elements, air and fire, which are weightless and rise; the four elements are the old Greek scheme.
Refers to the Ages of Man, declining from gold to iron, described earlier in the poem.
The Centaurs, wounded by Hercules' poisoned arrows, were said to have washed in the Anigros, tainting its water.
Pittheus was king of Trœzen and grandfather of Theseus; the hill is placed near his city.
"Horned Ammon" is the Libyan god Jupiter Ammon, shown with ram's horns; the water meant is his oracle's spring.
The son of Amithaon is the seer Melampus, who cured the daughters of Prœtus of madness.
The Symplegades were clashing rocks the Argonauts passed in the Argo; after that passage they stood fixed.
Pallene is a Thracian/Macedonian peninsula; the Tritonian lake is in Libya. The feathered-people tale is a traveller's legend that Pythagoras himself doubts.
The 'deadly moth' is the chrysalis-born moth; 'deadly' reflects the ancients' sense of it as a death-like change.
The peacock is Juno's bird, its tail marked with 'stars' (eyes); Cytherea is Venus, whose bird is the dove.
Amomum is an aromatic spice plant; frankincense is fragrant tree resin burned as incense.
Hyperion is the Sun god; his city is Heliopolis in Egypt, where the Phoenix was said to bring its parent's remains.
The animal living on wind and air is the chameleon, believed to take on the colour of whatever it touches.
Phœbus is the sun god, whose horses draw the sun's chariot; bathing them in the sea means sunset. The speaker, Pythagoras, says a day would not be long enough.
The citadel of Cecrops is Athens, whose legendary first king was Cecrops. The citadel of Amphion is Thebes, which he fortified with his lyre.
Dardanian means Trojan, from Dardanus, an ancestor of the Trojans. Rome is so called because Aeneas's Trojans were thought to have founded it.
Helenus was a Trojan prophet, son of Priam. Aeneas is addressed as 'Son of a Goddess' because his mother was Venus.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, used here for Troy itself.
Iülus was the son of Aeneas, and the Julian family, including Julius Caesar and Augustus, claimed descent from him. The prophecy points to Caesar or Augustus.
The Penates were household gods of Rome, which Aeneas carried from Troy. Pelasgians here means Greeks.
Thyestes was tricked into eating his own sons at a banquet. 'Victuals fit for Thyestes' means meat, equated with cannibalism.
Feather foils were lines strung with feathers that frightened deer into nets.

context_notes.text: Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome, famed for religious reforms. Ovid imagines him visiting Pythagoras at Crotona, a Greek city in southern Italy.
The Golden Age was the mythic first era of humanity, peaceful and plentiful, without war, toil or meat-eating.
Haruspices read the entrails of sacrificial animals to learn the gods' will, a common Roman divination practice.
Pythagoras is arguing for vegetarianism: if souls move between animals and humans, eating meat may mean eating kin.
The speaker is Pythagoras of Samos, a philosopher teaching Numa, who here sets out his doctrine of reincarnation and change.
Pythagoras is speaking, teaching that nothing truly dies but only changes form.
Helice and Buris were Achaian cities destroyed by an earthquake and flood in 373 BC.
Ætna is the volcano in Sicily, often explained in myth by a giant or Vulcan's forge beneath it.
Ancient belief held that bees spontaneously generated from bullock carcasses (bugonia); this was accepted natural lore, not a joke.
This is an ancient folk belief that bear cubs are born shapeless and licked into form.
The Phoenix is a mythical bird said to be reborn from its own ashes or body; Ovid's version is one of the earliest.
Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus) was said to have conquered India; the lynx was linked with his chariot, and 'lyncurium' stone was thought to be hardened lynx urine.
Troy fell after the ten-year Trojan War, fought over Helen.
Thebes was the city of Oedipus, whose tragic story was famous.
Pythagoras taught that souls transmigrate between humans and animals, which is why he urged vegetarianism.

literary_notes.text: Earth is portrayed as a generous giver who 'yields' and 'affords' food, a nurturing mother.
The opening 'Alas!' and the striking repetition of 'entrails' and 'living creature' dramatize his horror and stress the circular cruelty of eating flesh.
Questions piling up adjectives of innocence make the ox's slaughter seem a betrayal of a faithful servant.
The ox is honored with garlands and the grain it grew while being led to slaughter, which sharpens the pathos.
Pythagoras's imagined flight above the clouds elevates him as a visionary prophet looking down on foolish mortals.
Wax remolded into new shapes illustrates the soul keeping its identity through changing bodies.
Pythagoras compares his long discourse to a sea voyage under full sail.
Time is likened to a river whose waves push one another onward, illustrating ceaseless flux.
The year's four seasons are presented as the stages of a human life, from infancy to old age.
Winter is made an aged man with trembling steps and thinning or white hair.
Pythagoras addresses Time and Old Age directly, giving a grim, rhetorical close to the passage.
Birth and death are redefined as mere change, stating the philosophy of the whole poem.
Pythagoras addresses the ages directly, giving the decline from gold to iron solemn weight as an example of change.
Earth swollen by trapped winds is compared to a bladder or goatskin inflated by breath, making the geology vivid.
The earth is imagined as a living animal with lungs that grows hungry and abandons its flames.
Bees are given human traits: delight in toil and labouring in hope, making their generation from carcasses seem purposeful.
The mother 'forms' the cub like a sculptor shaping a body, turning birth into craftsmanship.
The aromatic nest and death amid sweet odours make the Phoenix's end a ritual, a symbol of renewal through death.
The dutiful carrying of cradle and sepulchre joins birth and death in one burden, echoing the book's theme of continual change.
The claim that a whole day would not suffice to list all changes stresses how universal change is.
Troy is treated as a person who points to her own ruins and tombs in place of her wealth.
Asking what remains of Athens besides its name makes the fall of great cities feel stark and certain.
Helenus's prediction inside Pythagoras's speech ties the theme of change to Rome's future greatness.
The emotional outcry and pathos of the crying calf and kid make killing animals seem close to murder.
Calling the distance to murder a short step is a quiet, stark warning.
